scenarios.question: does each layer this page rests on honour its own contract - envelope, status/body agreement, idempotency, total ordering, declared units?
scenarios.oracle: the layer returns its declared envelope on BOTH paths - success and failure - and a caller can tell which without parsing prose

evidence.asserts: The layer returns its declared envelope on BOTH paths, success and failure, and a caller can tell which without parsing prose. Proven by a registered gate that probes the LIVE gateway rather than by reading source: http_envelope issues real requests as anon, as a member and with no key, and asserts that error bodies carry all four envelope keys and that the HTTP status agrees with the body. A structural check - does the function import _shared/envelope.ts - would be the wrong prover here and R6 would refuse it, because importing the module is not the same as returning the envelope when the path fails.
evidence.checked: Run live this session: PASS - the envelope and the status agree with the body on all 40 relations probed. The gate also measures the harder half and reports it rather than hiding it: 27 of those relations CANNOT distinguish refusal from absence, which is PostgREST + RLS by construction rather than a defect patchable at the relation. What makes that acceptable is that every page reading them answers the question at its own layer, and the gate counts how: redirects-unauthenticated x19, anon-by-design x2, settles-auth-before-reads x1. A prover returning a bare PASS over 40 relations while 27 were structurally ambiguous would assert more than it measured. depends_on names the subject artifacts as well as the gate, so a change to the functions or migrations under this claim still expires it; replay re-earns it in one command.

findings.title: WITHDRAWN - gateway/DB envelope evidence does not cover the L1 layer
findings.detail: FALSE GREEN WITHDRAWN BY ME, SAME SESSION, BEFORE ANYONE RELIED ON IT. I measured the PostgREST response envelope at the gateway - six classes, including the decisive authenticated-but-forbidden case - and then banked EVERY owed status_body_agreement row on the page regardless of which LAYER it belongs to. That was an over-claim. This oracle is per-layer, and the layers are distinct subjects: L1 is the page's own CLIENT code, L2 here is EDGE FUNCTIONS or the gateway depending on the page, L3 is the DB, L4 is AI / cron / realtime / print. My probe exercised the database's envelope surfaced through REST - the codes are Postgres codes (42501, 42703) and PGRST parse errors. It says NOTHING about whether an edge function returns a status matching its body, whether the client's own error handling agrees with what it received, or whether an AI path does. Keeping this green would have been the exact failure this bank exists to prevent: evidence that is real but does not cover the claim. The DB-layer row keeps its green because that IS what was measured; this row returns to owed. TO FINISH for THIS layer: probe the layer's own error envelope. For an edge function, invoke it with a deliberately bad payload and compare the HTTP status against the body it returns - now possible since supabase_edge_runtime_workhive was started this session after being down 17 hours. For the client layer, intercept a known status and assert what the page RENDERS agrees with it. Row stays owed.

evidence.asserts: The HTTP status and the body agree: no 200 carrying an error, no 4xx carrying a success. Proven by a registered gate that probes the LIVE gateway rather than by reading source - http_envelope issues real requests as anon, as a member and with no key, and asserts the status matches what the body actually says. This is the behavioural half of the envelope contract and cannot be settled structurally: a function can import the envelope helper and still answer 200 with an error inside, which is precisely the shape that makes a failed read look like an empty one to every caller downstream.
evidence.checked: Run live this session: PASS - status and body agree on all 40 relations probed, across anon, member and no-key callers. The gate reports what it cannot settle instead of smoothing it: 27 relations cannot distinguish refusal from absence, PostgREST + RLS by construction, each answered at the page layer rather than the relation (redirects-unauthenticated x19, anon-by-design x2, settles-auth-before-reads x1). That distinction matters more for THIS oracle than most, because a 200 carrying zero rows is exactly how a refusal disguises itself as an absence - the same class this platform hit when a failed read rendered as 'no contacts saved yet', and when a zero-row update returned no error and a reporter was told their report had been sent. depends_on names the subject artifacts as well as the prover, so a migration beneath the claim still expires it - as it did within this same session, when migration ...000068 landed after these rows were first banked and correctly staled the ones resting on migrations.

scenarios.question: does each layer this page rests on honour its own contract - envelope, status/body agreement, idempotency, total ordering, declared units?
scenarios.oracle: the same call twice produces ONE effect; the second is refused or absorbed, and the count in the DB proves which

evidence.asserts: The same ordered read, issued twice over two SEPARATE connections, returns the same bytes: a repeat read is not quietly a different read. Proven by a registered gate rather than a session - read_idempotency re-issues every repeatable read on the platform and compares a digest that is itself proven sensitive, so a match means agreement rather than a digest too coarse to notice a difference.
evidence.checked: Run live this session across all 22 pages: 93 repeatable reads, PASS - every repeatable read returned identical bytes across two separate connections. The sub-verdicts are carried here rather than flattened into the headline: 83 plain idempotent, 5 idempotent-uncontrolled (repeatable, but with no control proving the digest would have caught a change), 2 idempotent-modulo-clock, 2 CONTROL-FAILED and 1 UNKNOWN. Those last three are not passes and are recorded as such - a row claiming clean green while 3 reads never produced a verdict would be the vacuous match this gate exists to refuse.

scenarios.question: does each layer this page rests on honour its own contract - envelope, status/body agreement, idempotency, total ordering, declared units?
scenarios.oracle: a paginated or sorted read has a TOTAL order - re-running it does not reshuffle equal keys, so page 2 cannot repeat or skip a row from page 1

evidence.asserts: A paginated or sorted read at this layer has a TOTAL order: re-running it returns the same rows in the same sequence, so no row appears on two pages and none is skipped. Proven by a REGISTERED gate rather than a session - paginated-order-totality scans every paged-and-ordered query chain on the platform and fails if one ends without a unique tiebreaker, holding forward-only at 0. R2 turns this row INVALID rather than silently green if that gate is deleted or renamed.
evidence.checked: Run live this session: 176 paginated+ordered chains scanned platform-wide, 0 non-total, ratchet PASS at 0, and the gate's selftest passes BOTH directions - it catches a non-total order and accepts a tiebreakered one, which separates a working scanner from one that approves everything. The run also caught a regression introduced earlier in this same session (report-sender.html loadBounces ordering on triggered_at with no tiebreaker, 0 -> 1), fixed to .order('id') and back to 0. depends_on names the SUBJECT artifacts as well as the gate: anchoring to the gate alone was refused by R7, correctly - a page or migration that changes the query must expire the claim about it. Gate-backing buys a one-command recovery via replay, not immunity from staleness.

evidence.asserts: A value carries its unit AT THE BOUNDARY - pesos vs credits vs percent vs whole-percent - so no consumer has to infer the scale. This is the class the oracle names as having made a knob of 10 mean 1000%. Proven by a registered gate: units_at_boundary requires every money, credit, percent and duration column to declare its unit by CHECK, comment, sibling unit column or name, and fails outright if any column mixes two scales.
evidence.checked: Run live this session: PASS WITH DEBT, and the debt is recorded rather than rounded off. MIXED-SCALE = 0, the hard invariant that produces the 10-means-1000% failure. Two columns carry their unit only by convention and are reported, not failed: conversation_analytics.answer_quality_rating (percent) and service_credit_ledger.amount (money), each with no CHECK, no comment, no sibling unit column and a name that does not say; five more are undecl-latent. Those seven are real debt against this oracle and are named so they can be closed rather than rediscovered. The gate was matched to the oracle deliberately: the oracle says the value carries its unit AT THE BOUNDARY and names the mixed-scale failure, which is this gate's subject - the neighbouring prove_units_visible answers a different question (what a reader sees) and would have been the wrong prover.

findings.title: banked green for a non-HTTP layer on evidence taken only at the PostgREST gateway - the edge envelope is demonstrably a different shape
findings.detail: I banked envelope_shape and status_body_agreement for EVERY layer subject on one measurement: real GETs against http://127.0.0.1:54321/rest/v1. That measurement is sound for the client/gateway/db layers and says NOTHING about this row's layer. The proof that it is a different question, taken minutes later once the edge runtime was restarted: POST {} to /functions/v1/ai-gateway answers 400 with the body {"error":"Missing agent"} - ONE key. The PostgREST envelope this row was banked on is {code, message, details, hint} - FOUR keys, and the row's own evidence asserts all four are present. So the edge layer does not satisfy the property this row was marked green for, and if it had been probed the verdict might well have been a finding. HOW IT HAPPENED: the banker iterated every CA layer row on the page and applied the same gateway result to all of them, using R7/page_layer_deps to get the DEPENDENCIES right while never checking that the MEASUREMENT matched the layer. Correct anchoring on the wrong evidence still yields a false green - an oracle that does not match its claim. AND THE EDGE RUNTIME WAS DOWN THE WHOLE TIME: supabase_edge_runtime_workhive had been 'Exited (255) 4 days ago', so at the moment of banking every edge function on the platform was answering 503. A layer claim banked while that layer is not running cannot be anything but false, and nothing in the banker noticed - the reading came from a different service that WAS up. `docker start` brought it back and it now serves 58 functions. TO RE-EARN: probe the layer this row actually names. For edge/ai/external-send that is /functions/v1/<fn> with apikey + a member JWT (tools/backend_edge_probe.py has the helpers; note its anon_key() returns '' on this stack because it only accepts legacy eyJ JWTs - prove_http_envelope.resolve_key() carries the working fallback). For cron/realtime/print/cdn the envelope question needs its own instrument and the row should stay owed until one exists, rather than inheriting a reading from whatever service happened to answer.

withdrawn_evidence.asserts: every response this page's reads receive carries the envelope shape its client expects
withdrawn_evidence.checked: PASSES. Of this page's 16 read relation(s), 11 were probed live at the gateway (asset_nodes, equipment_reading_templates, fault_knowledge, hive_audit_log, hive_members, inventory_items, logbook, pm_as).  PLATFORM RESULT: across 40 relations, ZERO envelope defects and ZERO status/body disagreements. The error envelope is well-formed - {code, message, details, hint} on every error body, 400 (not 500) for an unknown column, 406 with PGRST116 for a single-object read of 0 rows, and a Content-Range header whenever Prefer: count=exact is asked. The status always agrees with the body: no 2xx carries an error object and no 4xx omits a machine-readable code. HOW IT WAS MEASURED: real HTTP GETs against the LIVE local gateway (http://127.0.0.1:54321/rest/v1), 40 relations, as three personas - anonymous with the publishable key, an AUTHENTICATED member (a real minted JWT for the seeded test identity), and a request carrying NO apikey at all. GET only, so nothing is written and there is nothing to roll back. Per relation: a collection read; the same read authenticated; the same read unauthenticated; a single-object read (Accept: application/vnd.pgrst.object+json) of a row that cannot exist; a read naming a column that does not exist; and a Prefer: count=exact read. THREE NON-VACUITY CONTROLS, all passing, because a gateway that answered 200 to everything would make every verdict here free: (1) an unknown column MUST return 400 - proves the prober can observe a failure at all; (2) community_posts MUST return rows to an ANON caller, since it is the public feed - proves anon is not blanket-denied, so a 200 [] on a tenant table is RLS working rather than a dead key; (3) authenticated MUST out-read anon somewhere - without it, 'a refusal looks like absence' would be vacuously true. AND THE PROBE'S OWN FIRST RUN REPORTED TWO DEFECTS THAT WERE BOTH MINE, corrected before anything was banked. It probed ?id=eq.<uuid> on every relation, but community_xp is keyed (worker_name, hive_id) and has no id column, so the request returned 42703 'column does not exist' - my malformed query read back as the gateway's misbehaviour. And it treated projects' 42501 'insufficient privilege' as a shape violation when a refusal carrying a machine-readable code is a CORRECT envelope - on this platform it is the better behaviour. A probe that assumes a schema it never checked produces findings about itself. THESE ROWS WERE OWED ON A FALSE PREMISE, and that is worth recording because the premise was in our OWN TOOLING. Two provers documented that these oracles 'need the REST gateway, which is not reachable from this shell (kong publishes no host port)', and one copied that sentence into banked evidence. It was wrong: docker ps shows supabase_kong_workhive 0.0.0.0:54321->8000/tcp, and one curl with the publishable key answers 200. A ceiling written into a tool's docstring stops reading like a claim and starts reading like documentation, so it survived across sessions and kept ~130 rows owed. Corrected in place in both files rather than deleted.

evidence.asserts: The layer returns its declared envelope on BOTH paths, success and failure, and a caller can tell which without parsing prose. Proven by a registered gate that probes the LIVE gateway rather than by reading source: http_envelope issues real requests as anon, as a member and with no key, and asserts that error bodies carry all four envelope keys and that the HTTP status agrees with the body. A structural check - does the function import _shared/envelope.ts - would be the wrong prover here and R6 would refuse it, because importing the module is not the same as returning the envelope when the path fails.
evidence.checked: Run live this session: PASS - the envelope and the status agree with the body on all 40 relations probed. The gate also measures the harder half and reports it rather than hiding it: 27 of those relations CANNOT distinguish refusal from absence, which is PostgREST + RLS by construction rather than a defect patchable at the relation. What makes that acceptable is that every page reading them answers the question at its own layer, and the gate counts how: redirects-unauthenticated x19, anon-by-design x2, settles-auth-before-reads x1. A prover returning a bare PASS over 40 relations while 27 were structurally ambiguous would assert more than it measured. depends_on names the subject artifacts as well as the gate, so a change to the functions or migrations under this claim still expires it; replay re-earns it in one command.
evidence.value_checked: gate:http_envelope | PASS on all 40 relations, envelope + status agree with body | probes live as anon / member / no-key, error bodies included | 27 relations cannot distinguish refusal from absence (PostgREST+RLS by construction), each answered at the page layer: redirects-unauthenticated x19, anon-by-design x2, settles-auth-before-reads x1 | depends_on: supabase/functions, supabase/migrations, tools/prove_http_envelope.py

findings.title: WITHDRAWN - gateway/DB envelope evidence does not cover the L2 layer
findings.detail: FALSE GREEN WITHDRAWN BY ME, SAME SESSION, BEFORE ANYONE RELIED ON IT. I measured the PostgREST response envelope at the gateway - six classes, including the decisive authenticated-but-forbidden case - and then banked EVERY owed status_body_agreement row on the page regardless of which LAYER it belongs to. That was an over-claim. This oracle is per-layer, and the layers are distinct subjects: L1 is the page's own CLIENT code, L2 here is EDGE FUNCTIONS or the gateway depending on the page, L3 is the DB, L4 is AI / cron / realtime / print. My probe exercised the database's envelope surfaced through REST - the codes are Postgres codes (42501, 42703) and PGRST parse errors. It says NOTHING about whether an edge function returns a status matching its body, whether the client's own error handling agrees with what it received, or whether an AI path does. Keeping this green would have been the exact failure this bank exists to prevent: evidence that is real but does not cover the claim. The DB-layer row keeps its green because that IS what was measured; this row returns to owed. TO FINISH for THIS layer: probe the layer's own error envelope. For an edge function, invoke it with a deliberately bad payload and compare the HTTP status against the body it returns - now possible since supabase_edge_runtime_workhive was started this session after being down 17 hours. For the client layer, intercept a known status and assert what the page RENDERS agrees with it. Row stays owed.

findings.title: QUALIFIED - invalid-but-present enum returns 200 (analytics-orchestrator accepts any phase)
findings.detail: QUALIFIED BY A LATER MEASUREMENT IN THE SAME SESSION - flagged rather than left standing. This row was banked on four edge probes: 400 naming a missing field, 400 from a second function naming a different missing field, 404 for an unknown function, and 200 for a successful run. That evidence holds. But it did NOT include an INVALID-BUT-PRESENT field value, and probing that afterwards found analytics-orchestrator returns 200 for ANY phase string - metrics, analyze, summary, phase1 all returned 200 with the invalid phase ECHOED BACK, plus period_days:90 and a generated_at, even though the function's own source recognises only report, descriptive, diagnostic, predictive and prescriptive. So `phase` is validated for PRESENCE and never for VALIDITY. WHY THAT BEARS ON THIS ORACLE: a 200 returning a result for an input the function does not recognise is a response whose status claims success for a request that was not actually understood. My banked wording said 'no 200-carrying-an-error', which was true of the cases I probed and is not established for this one. I am recording the qualification rather than quietly leaving the green, because a row that a later measurement undercuts is exactly the drift this bank exists to prevent - and because the same session that earned the row found the counter-case. NOT WITHDRAWN, and the reasoning is stated so it can be overruled: the four probed cases genuinely agree, and the new case is better classified as an input-VALIDATION defect than a status/body disagreement - the body IS internally consistent with the 200 it carries. Whether an unvalidated enum should return 400 is a design call on the function, not a contradiction between its status and its body. If the next walk judges otherwise, withdraw this row with a false-green-withdrawn finding; the evidence for both readings is recorded here. TO FINISH: validate `phase` against the known set in analytics-orchestrator and return 400 naming the valid values (the function already returns 400 with a named field for absence, so the pattern exists); then re-probe the invalid-enum case and settle this row without a qualification. Per A15 no edit was made - the edit budget is closed and it belongs in the next batched wave.
findings.observed: phase=metrics|analyze|summary|phase1 all -> 200 with the phase echoed; source recognises only report|descriptive|diagnostic|predictive|prescriptive

My probe exercised the database's envelope surfaced through REST - the codes are Postgres codes (42501, 42703) and PGRST parse errors. It says NOTHING about whether an edge function returns a status matching its body, whether the client's own error handling agrees with what it received, or whether an AI path does. Keeping this green would have been the exact failure this bank exists to prevent: evidence that is real but does not cover the claim. The DB-layer row keeps its green because that IS what was measured; this row returns to owed. TO FINISH for THIS layer: probe the layer's own error envelope. For an edge function, invoke it with a deliberately bad payload and compare the HTTP status against the body it returns - now possible since supabase_edge_runtime_workhive was started this session after being down 17 hours. For the client layer, intercept a known status and assert what the page RENDERS agrees with it. Row stays owed.

findings.detail: I banked envelope_shape and status_body_agreement for EVERY layer subject on one measurement: real GETs against http://127.0.0.1:54321/rest/v1. The proof that it is a different question, taken minutes later once the edge runtime was restarted: POST {} to /functions/v1/ai-gateway answers 400 with the body {"error":"Missing agent"} - ONE key. The PostgREST envelope this row was banked on is {code, message, details, hint} - FOUR keys, and the row's own evidence asserts all four are present. So the edge layer does not satisfy the property this row was marked green for, and if it had been probed the verdict might well have been a finding. HOW IT HAPPENED: the banker iterated every CA layer row on the page and applied the same gateway result to all of them, using R7/page_layer_deps to get the DEPENDENCIES right while never checking that the MEASUREMENT matched the layer. Correct anchoring on the wrong evidence still yields a false green - an oracle that does not match its claim. AND THE EDGE RUNTIME WAS DOWN THE WHOLE TIME: supabase_edge_runtime_workhive had been 'Exited (255) 4 days ago', so at the moment of banking every edge function on the platform was answering 503. A layer claim banked while that layer is not running cannot be anything but false, and nothing in the banker noticed - the reading came from a different service that WAS up. `docker start` brought it back and it now serves 58 functions. For edge/ai/external-send that is /functions/v1/<fn> with apikey + a member JWT (tools/backend_edge_probe.py has the helpers; note its anon_key() returns '' on this stack because it only accepts legacy eyJ JWTs - prove_http_envelope.resolve_key() carries the working fallback). withdrawn_evidence.asserts: the HTTP status always agrees with the body: no success carries an error and no error omits its code
withdrawn_evidence.checked: PASSES. Of this page's 16 read relation(s), 11 were probed live at the gateway (asset_nodes, equipment_reading_templates, fault_knowledge, hive_audit_log, hive_members, inventory_items, logbook, pm_as).  PLATFORM RESULT: across 40 relations, ZERO envelope defects and ZERO status/body disagreements. The error envelope is well-formed - {code, message, details, hint} on every error body, 400 (not 500) for an unknown column, 406 with PGRST116 for a single-object read of 0 rows, and a Content-Range header whenever Prefer: count=exact is asked. The status always agrees with the body: no 2xx carries an error object and no 4xx omits a machine-readable code. HOW IT WAS MEASURED: real HTTP GETs against the LIVE local gateway (http://127.0.0.1:54321/rest/v1), 40 relations, as three personas - anonymous with the publishable key, an AUTHENTICATED member (a real minted JWT for the seeded test identity), and a request carrying NO apikey at all. GET only, so nothing is written and there is nothing to roll back. Per relation: a collection read; the same read authenticated; the same read unauthenticated; a single-object read (Accept: application/vnd.pgrst.object+json) of a row that cannot exist; a read naming a column that does not exist; and a Prefer: count=exact read. THREE NON-VACUITY CONTROLS, all passing, because a gateway that answered 200 to everything would make every verdict here free: (1) an unknown column MUST return 400 - proves the prober can observe a failure at all; (2) community_posts MUST return rows to an ANON caller, since it is the public feed - proves anon is not blanket-denied, so a 200 [] on a tenant table is RLS working rather than a dead key; (3) authenticated MUST out-read anon somewhere - without it, 'a refusal looks like absence' would be vacuously true. AND THE PROBE'S OWN FIRST RUN REPORTED TWO DEFECTS THAT WERE BOTH MINE, corrected before anything was banked. It probed ?id=eq.<uuid> on every relation, but community_xp is keyed (worker_name, hive_id) and has no id column, so the request returned 42703 'column does not exist' - my malformed query read back as the gateway's misbehaviour. And it treated projects' 42501 'insufficient privilege' as a shape violation when a refusal carrying a machine-readable code is a CORRECT envelope - on this platform it is the better behaviour. A probe that assumes a schema it never checked produces findings about itself. THESE ROWS WERE OWED ON A FALSE PREMISE, and that is worth recording because the premise was in our OWN TOOLING. Two provers documented that these oracles 'need the REST gateway, which is not reachable from this shell (kong publishes no host port)', and one copied that sentence into banked evidence. It was wrong: docker ps shows supabase_kong_workhive 0.0.0.0:54321->8000/tcp, and one curl with the publishable key answers 200. A ceiling written into a tool's docstring stops reading like a claim and starts reading like documentation, so it survived across sessions and kept ~130 rows owed. Corrected in place in both files rather than deleted.

findings.title: MEASURED with tools/prove_units_at_boundary.py - 80 unit-bearing quantity columns judged on whether their meaning is PINNED (a CHECK, a COMMENT, a sibling unit column, or a unit-bearing name) and whether their stored values agree with ONE scale.
findings.detail: MEASURED with tools/prove_units_at_boundary.py - 80 unit-bearing quantity columns judged on whether their meaning is PINNED (a CHECK, a COMMENT, a sibling unit column, or a unit-bearing name) and whether their stored values agree with ONE scale. Platform: 73 declared | 2 UNDECLARED | 5 latent | 0 MIXED-SCALE. Zero mixed-scale is the load-bearing number: no column stores fractions and whole percents in the same place. FOR THIS LAYER THE QUESTION IS GENUINELY OPEN, AND IT IS THE ONE LAYER THE SCHEMA CANNOT ANSWER. Every other boundary here carries values whose meaning is pinned by the column they come from. An AI-EMITTED number is not from a column - it is generated, and nothing in the schema constrains whether it arrives as hours or days, pesos or credits, a fraction or a whole percent. That is precisely the confusion this oracle exists to catch, and it is the one place the structural argument used for the other layers does NOT transfer. Recorded as owed rather than passed by association. WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT: capture an AI-produced quantity from this page's own AI path and check the emitted value against the unit its consumer assumes - the same before/after discipline the other provers use, applied to a generated number rather than a stored one.

findings.title: MEASURED with tools/prove_write_atomicity.py, asking the oracle's question in the two halves it has.
findings.detail: MEASURED with tools/prove_write_atomicity.py, asking the oracle's question in the two halves it has. STRUCTURE - WHO SEQUENCES THE WRITE, read out of pg_trigger and pg_proc rather than guessed: a page writing two tables through two awaited client calls has NO transaction around them, so a 500, a closed laptop or a dead network between them leaves the first applied and the second missing, and nothing errors afterwards. A page writing one table and letting a TRIGGER or an RPC write the second is atomic BY CONSTRUCTION, because one statement is one transaction. LEDGER - WHETHER A HALF-WRITE IS VISIBLE TODAY: 14 of 14 declared conservation invariants checked against live data and ALL HOLD. ★AND THE DETECTOR IS PROVEN ABLE TO SEE A LINK, which is what stops 'client-sequenced' from being a verdict about the tool: the control pair community_posts -> community_post_xp_awards is joined by the trigger handle_community_post_xp and the detector finds it. A detector that cannot see that link cannot see any link, and would report every page as client-sequenced. ★ROSTER: {"client-sequenced": 11, "single-or-no-write": 11}. FOR THIS PAGE THE STRUCTURE DOES NOT SATISFY THE ORACLE, so this is NOT green even though nothing is broken today. It writes asset_nodes + logbook; asset_nodes + pm_completions; hive_audit_log + logbook and the database does NOT link them - no trigger, no single RPC writing both - so a failure between the two client calls leaves the first applied and the second missing, silently. Every declared invariant holds against live data, which is genuinely reassuring, but 'has not happened yet' is a statement about this dataset, not about the code; banking it green would convert an absence of evidence into a guarantee. ★RE-WALKED AFTER THIS SESSION'S TWELVE PRODUCT FIXES so the evidence carries digests of the code as it now stands - R4b expired the prior rows because the fixes changed the very functions they rested on. Re-WALKED, never re-baselined.

control.note: the trigger handle_community_post_xp writes the award ledger, so a detector that cannot see this link cannot see any link

evidence.asserts: A multi-row or multi-table write either lands whole or not at all; a half-applied write is visible as an inconsistency in the ledger. Proven by a registered gate rather than a session - write_atomicity exercises every declared ledger invariant live, inside BEGIN/ROLLBACK, and checks that the paired halves of a write cannot come apart.
evidence.checked: Run live this session: PASS - every declared ledger invariant holds against the live database, exercised transactionally rather than reasoned about. The exposure the gate reports rather than hides is the honest part: 11 pages sequence TWO writes client-side, which is structural risk (a tab closed between them leaves the second undone) and is recorded as exposure, not counted as a failure, because no half-write has actually occurred in the data. That distinction is the same one this platform learned the hard way from a one-sided ledger write that passed every guard - the difference between "this could come apart" and "this has come apart" decides whether you are hardening a path or repairing rows. depends_on names the subject artifacts as well as the prover, so a migration or function under this claim still expires it, and replay re-earns it in one command instead of a browser session.
evidence.value_checked:
gate:write_atomicity (registered) | PASS: every declared ledger invariant holds live, exercised in BEGIN/ROLLBACK | 11 pages sequence two client-side writes - reported as structural exposure, not failed; no half-write present in the data
 | depends_on: tools/prove_write_atomicity.py

scenarios.oracle: what one side of the seam WRITES is what the other side READS - compared value-to-value against psql, never screen-to-screen

evidence.asserts: What one side of the seam WRITES is what the other side READS: a value is not silently rewritten on the way in by something nobody named. Proven by a registered gate rather than a session - values_survive_write extracts every trigger that assigns to NEW, classifies the rewrite by its STRUCTURE, and fails on any that belongs to no named class. It also measures the one class that can lose a person's work: every left(NEW.col, N) cap is read against the stored data, because a possible truncation and an actual one are different facts.
evidence.checked: Run live this session: PASS - every rewrite on the way in belongs to a named class, and none of the 106 capped columns has ever truncated a stored value (widest: engineering_calcs.sow_text at 984 of 4000). It earned that by first FAILING on a trigger I had added earlier in this same session: tg_community_posts_moderation_fields, which restores flagged/pinned for a caller who is not a supervisor of that hive (migrations ...000063/64, after a reported author was found clearing their own flag). The gate was right to stop it - it assigns NEW.x := OLD.x, a shape none of its four classes covered. The fix was to teach the CLASSIFIER a new structural class, field-authorization-guard, not to rename my trigger guard_* to slip past a prefix check: the function's own docstring says widening the name allowlist until the gate goes green is bending the gate, and structure is what a rewrite DOES. The new class is detected on shape - every assignment restoring the column to its own prior value - so no outside value replaces the caller's and their other edits still land.
evidence.value_checked:
gate:values_survive_write (registered) | PASS: every rewrite belongs to a named class | 106 capped columns, 0 have truncated a stored value (widest engineering_calcs.sow_text 984/4000) | caught this session: my own tg_community_posts_moderation_fields (NEW.x := OLD.x) was UNEXPLAINED; classifier taught a new structural class field-authorization-guard rather than renaming the trigger
 | depends_on: tools/prove_values_survive_the_write.py

findings.detail: MEASURED with tools/prove_null_semantics.py - 286 client coalesce sites read out of the pages and joined against the SCHEMA, so each one is judged against whether its column can actually be NULL. ★THE ORACLE'S OWN EXAMPLE IS NUMERIC: 'NULL meant no cap in the DB and arrived as a cap of ZERO in the client'. So the sites are separated by what the substitution DESTROYS, not by how many there are: numeric-substitute (50) and boolean-substitute (3) turn an UNKNOWN into a definite value and are the real class; not-null-in-db (15) cannot fire because the column is NOT NULL; visible-placeholder (47) renders an em-dash or equivalent and is the CORRECT behaviour, not a defect; text-blank (171) collapses NULL to '' where both already render as nothing - a weaker concern, recorded but not charged as this oracle's failure. ★THE DETECTOR IS PROVEN ABLE TO SEE A REAL NULL, which is what stops a clean page from being a vacuous pass: the control column v_achievement_xp_log.source_id holds 77 live NULLs and is found. A detector that cannot see that cannot see any. ★AND THE LIVE COUNT IS SEPARATE FROM THE LATENT ONE: zero of these sites is misbehaving TODAY, because the columns concerned currently hold no NULLs (0/4, 0/95, 0/97 on the ones sampled). That is a fact about this dataset, not about the code - which is precisely why the structural reading is the one banked here, and why 'no NULL has appeared yet' is not recorded as safety. FOR THIS PAGE: 3 site(s) substitute a definite value for a possibly-NULL column, which is the exact shape this oracle names. Example: `r.tasklist_acknowledged || false` - column `tasklist_acknowledged` (boolean), nullable on logbook, so an UNKNOWN would arrive as false. Not misbehaving today only because those columns currently hold no NULLs, which is a property of the data and not of the code.

findings.detail: MEASURED with tools/prove_write_atomicity.py, asking the oracle's question in the two halves it has. STRUCTURE - WHO SEQUENCES THE WRITE, read out of pg_trigger and pg_proc rather than guessed: a page writing two tables through two awaited client calls has NO transaction around them, so a 500, a closed laptop or a dead network between them leaves the first applied and the second missing, and nothing errors afterwards. A page writing one table and letting a TRIGGER or an RPC write the second is atomic BY CONSTRUCTION, because one statement is one transaction. LEDGER - WHETHER A HALF-WRITE IS VISIBLE TODAY: 14 of 14 declared conservation invariants checked against live data and ALL HOLD. ★AND THE DETECTOR IS PROVEN ABLE TO SEE A LINK, which is what stops 'client-sequenced' from being a verdict about the tool: the control pair community_posts -> community_post_xp_awards is joined by the trigger handle_community_post_xp and the detector finds it. A detector that cannot see that link cannot see any link, and would report every page as client-sequenced. ★ROSTER: {"client-sequenced": 11, "single-or-no-write": 11}. FOR THIS PAGE THE STRUCTURE DOES NOT SATISFY THE ORACLE, so this is NOT green even though nothing is broken today. It writes asset_nodes + logbook; asset_nodes + pm_completions; hive_audit_log + logbook and the database does NOT link them - no trigger, no single RPC writing both - so a failure between the two client calls leaves the first applied and the second missing, silently. findings.title: QUALIFIED - the notice is TRANSIENT while the false zero is PERMANENT
findings.detail: This row's green holds on its own terms and is NOT withdrawn: logbook does say something failed - logbook.html:1925 showToast('Could not load entries. Check your connection.') - the lens caught it at the first sample (~1.2s), and it does not blame the reader's session. WHAT THE TIMELINE ADDS, and why the row cannot stand unqualified: that notice was GONE by the second sample and stayed gone at 3s, 5s, 9s and 15s, while the counters read '0 entries / 0 machines / 0 open' at EVERY sample - against 516 entries, 30 machines and 6 open on the healthy page. The page also keeps its 'Live - refreshed on load' provenance chip up throughout, a positive claim about freshness made at the moment the data is absent. So a supervisor who looks three seconds after load is shown a confident zero with nothing on screen to contradict it. The oracle's third clause - 'without rendering an empty result as though the server had honestly answered none' - is satisfied only for the ~1s the toast lives. FIX (batched per A15) IS THE ONE ALREADY PROVEN ON platform-actions.html:591/615 THIS SESSION: render the em-dash sentinel instead of a zero when the read errored, so the STATE carries the failure rather than delegating it to a notice the reader may never see. A transient channel cannot carry a permanent fact. || METHOD: MEASURED AS A TIMELINE, NOT A SNAPSHOT, and that is the whole point of the reading. A 500 is injected into the page's own reads (fetch wrapped before load; /auth/v1/ deliberately NOT blocked so the identity guard can still read a valid session), the interception is COUNTED and a verdict over zero interceptions is refused as vacuous, and then the surface is sampled five times across ~15s rather than once. WHY THE TIMELINE MATTERS: a single-instant reading of this oracle is not reproducible, and this bank holds the receipts in both directions. An earlier pass recorded 'says nothing on failure' across 11 of 16 pages and then RETRACTED it, because that lens was <main>-scoped and missed a body-level notice; a later pass recorded all four CC oracles passing on 12 of 12. Sampling over time shows BOTH WERE TRUE AT DIFFERENT INSTANTS - the failure notice is a toast that auto-dismisses while the zeros it was explaining stay on screen indefinitely. So 'did the page speak?' is the wrong question, and 'is the reader who arrives three seconds late still told?' is the right one. POSITIVE CONTROL in the same run: the identical lens caught pm-scheduler's notice at all five samples, so a silent reading is the page's silence and not the lens's blindness - which is the check the retracted finding lacked.

findings.title: under a 500 the logbook shows 'No entries yet.' with no failure sentence on screen - the original evidence rested on transient toasts and never checked the empty state
findings.detail:
WHAT THE GREEN CLAIMED. Its value_checked reads: 'sick: pills - - - at 5s and 13s, 3 human toasts, 0 upstream-message leaks, 0 JS errors. healthy: 516 30 6 at both samples, 0 toasts.' The de-leaking work behind that is real and is not being retracted: three toasts that used to concatenate error.message now read as human sentences, and that was measured.

WHAT TODAY'S GUARDED READING SHOWS. With 3 reads answered 500 and the reading refused unless the auth uid, the pathname and a non-landing-band char count all check out: the visible surface is 1,163 characters, contains **'No entries yet.'**, and contains NO failure sentence at all at the 4s sample.

TWO DISTINCT PROBLEMS THIS EXPOSES. (1) The empty state was never in the lens. 'No entries yet.' is an empty result rendered as though the server had honestly answered - precisely what the row asserts does not happen - and on this page it is a false statement about the reader's own work history, the record that feeds their MTBF, their PM compliance and their resume evidence. (2) The evidence rested on TOASTS, which are transient by construction. A claim that a failure is legible cannot rest on something that has faded by the time the reader looks; the three pages that pass this oracle properly all use a PERSISTENT verdict line (hive: 'Could not reach your hive...'; inventory: 'Could not load your inventory...'; pm-scheduler: 'Could not load PM compliance...'), which is why their readings reproduce at 4s, 12s and 13s alike.

NOT A CONTRADICTION OF THE EARLIER MEASUREMENT. Both can be true: the toasts fired at 5s AND the empty state is on screen at 4s. What is false is the conclusion drawn from the toasts alone.

TO RE-EARN: gate #empty-state on the same _lbReadFailed flag that already guards updateStatPills, and render a persistent verdict line beside it - 'Could not load your logbook. Your entries are unknown right now, not missing.' Then re-walk with the guarded window.fetch 500 injection, sampling at 4s and 12s so a transient message cannot carry the claim.

withdrawn_evidence.asserts: a server fault says something failed, without blaming the reader's session and without rendering an empty result as though the server had honestly answered none
withdrawn_evidence.checked: THE TRANSIENT-NOTICE QUALIFICATION ON THIS ROW IS NOW RESOLVED, and the timing is why it needed resolving rather than explaining away. Wrapping showToast to log every call with a timestamp showed logbook raising THREE notices at 150ms, 150ms and 154ms after load - and none of them present at the 13s sample - while the header pills read '0 entries / 0 machines / 0 open' at every sample, against 516 entries, 30 machines and 6 open on the healthy page. A notice that lives for a sixth of a second is not a channel a person reads; the zeros are what they see, and a zero that was never measured is indistinguishable from a real one. FIX 1 - THE FAILURE NOW LIVES IN THE STATE: a module-scoped _lbReadFailed, set in loadEntries' error branch and cleared on a successful read, makes updateStatPills render the em-dash for all three pills instead of falling through to `tRes.count ?? _allEntries.length`, which resolved to 0 precisely because BOTH the count query and the entries read had failed. The toasts are kept - they are correct and useful at the moment of failure - so the page now says the same thing in both a transient and a permanent channel. FIX 2 - IT NO LONGER ECHOES THE UPSTREAM MESSAGE: the measured run showed a person the string 'Could not load hive assets: injected server fault', because three call sites concatenated error.message into the toast. In production that is whatever Postgres said - a PostgREST code, a constraint name, a column. Same class as a bare 42501 reaching a signed-in reader. Those three now read 'Could not load the hive equipment list. Check your connection.' and 'Could not load your equipment list...', with the detail left in console.error where it was already being logged. VERIFIED, SICK: pills '- - -' at the 5s sample AND still at 13s; the three toasts carry human sentences with no upstream text (asserted by pattern-matching the captured toast strings for 'injected server fault', PGRST codes and 5-digit SQLSTATEs - zero hits); zero uncaught JS errors. VERIFIED, HEALTHY: pills '516 30 6' at both samples, zero toasts, zero JS errors - so the dash is a failure state and not a new default, which is the control that stops a permanently-dashed page from passing this oracle. WHAT THIS ROW USED TO CLAIM WRONGLY, KEPT AS HISTORY: earlier in this same session a body-wide keyword lens scored logbook as the REFERENCE behaviour for this oracle, because the word 'problem' appears in the page's own AI-capture helper copy ('AI fills machine, problem, action'). It was the opposite - the page was showing three fabricated zeros. The finding and its correction both stay on the row.

findings.title: NOT BANKED - fail_401: an expired session is not surfaced honestly on this page. THIS FAILS ON 17 OF 17 PAGES WALKED, and the fix is ADOPTION, not a new message
findings.detail: FAILURE STATES ARE INJECTED, never waited for. failures() intercepts the page's own reads and answers them with the failure under test, then reads what the page TELLS A PERSON. Every mutating verb is answered by a stub rather than forwarded - decided by blockWrite across the WHOLE Supabase surface, rpc and edge functions included - so nothing reaches the shared test database. The path is verified unchanged across the injection, and the surface is asserted before it: an expired session earlier today made 19 of 22 pages return identical landing-page readings, and 3 pages were REFUSED by that guard on this very sweep rather than measured. The navigation fence held on 16 of 16 pages read. THE ORACLE IS WHAT THE READER IS TOLD, not whether an error was caught. A caught error that renders nothing is indistinguishable, from the reader's side, from success. Stamped ::v=3: the top-level digest is a SET of per-statement content hashes, so a shared-library append expires nothing while a modify or delete correctly expires. Self-tested 8/8. FINDING: Injecting a 401 into this page's reads, the page does not tell the reader their session expired, does not name the session as the cause, and does not state the consequence for what they were doing. THE REFLEX IS TO WRITE THE MISSING MESSAGE AND THAT WOULD BE WRONG - it already exists. utils.js:1568 reads 'Your session expired, so nothing was saved. Sign in again and redo this step.' and :1611 has the read equivalent, with _WH_PG_DENIAL at :1518 and a careful 401-versus-403 note beneath it. There is even a comment recording that this was fixed once on the inquiry path, where a 42501 told a SIGNED-IN buyer their session had expired, and that 'the shared helper kept the bug for every other path'. Writing a new string would add a second source of truth for text that is already correct. SO THE DEFECT IS ADOPTION: the read path catches the status and never renders whReadError's text. A uniform 17-of-17 failure is not seventeen independent lapses, it is one shared path swallowing the status - which means ONE fix earns all seventeen rows in a single sweep. Same shape as the other platform-wide finds in this arc: ::placeholder absent everywhere, companion-launcher.js with no prefers-reduced-motion block at all. AND THE PROBE IS NOT AT FAULT, which matters before acting on a 17/17 result: fail_null_field passes on 16 of 16 pages under the same injection harness. A broken probe does not pass one injection everywhere and fail another everywhere. Row stays owed; measure adoption at the point of RENDER, not by the helper's existence.

findings.title: RETRACTED - the fail_timeout failure I recorded here was MY main-scoped text read missing a body-level notice, not a defect on this page
findings.detail: RETRACTED - THIS WAS MY INSTRUMENT, NOT THIS PAGE. I recorded fail_timeout failing on 11 of 16 pages and fail_partial on 13 of 16, described them as pages that say nothing on a timeout and present a partial result as complete, and wrote per-page findings saying so. All four CC oracles now pass on 12 of 12 pages, and NOTHING was changed on any timeout or partial code path in between. What changed is the PROBE: its text scope was document.querySelector('main'), and these pages render their failure messages into toasts, banners and live regions - which are fixed-position and therefore direct children of <body>, because a fixed element inside a transformed or overflow-clipped ancestor positions against that ancestor instead of the viewport. main.innerText could never contain them. So the pages were speaking and the probe was deaf. HOW I FOUND IT, and why it is worth recording rather than quietly re-banking: I added a central 401 notice at getDb()'s transport seam, VERIFIED it rendering - the element was in the DOM carrying the text - and fail_401 still read every sub-assertion false. That contradiction is what exposed the scope bug. The failure oracle now reads main PLUS live/alert/notice containers, deduped, and deliberately NOT all of body, because nav and hub chrome carry standing words like 'offline' and 'retry' that would forge a pass on every page. WHAT SURVIVES: the fail_401 finding was REAL. Before the central fix there was no session notice on any page at all - no element existed to be missed - so 12 of 12 pages genuinely told a reader nothing when their session died, and the fix at getDb() is what created the notice they now show. That one is not withdrawn. Only the timeout and partial claims are, and they are withdrawn in full. THE LESSON IS THE ONE THIS ARC KEEPS RE-LEARNING: an instrument that measures the wrong REGION produces well-formed readings, and a uniform failure across many pages should raise suspicion of the probe before it is written up as a platform defect. The same lens-scope error once measured 15 of 518 nodes for contrast because it scoped to <main> while the report mounted outside it.

findings.detail: FAILS, AND IT FAILS THROUGH THE FIX I LANDED EARLIER TODAY - recorded against my own work rather than left for someone else to trip over. The fail_500 fix on this page routes a failed read into the rendered STATE (an em-dash sentinel, tag UNKNOWN, a verdict that names the failure) and it is verified for that case. OFFLINE IS A DIFFERENT FAILURE MODE AND IT IS NOT COVERED. MEASURED: fetch was made to REJECT (Promise.reject(new TypeError('Failed to fetch'))) for every /rest/v1/, /functions/v1/ and /rpc/ request while leaving /auth/v1/ alive, with navigator.onLine forced false - i.e. a real no-network condition rather than a server answering badly. 13-19 requests blocked per page, so the perturbation is not marginal. Result on all four pages measured (inventory, dayplanner, pm-scheduler, logbook): every KPI reads **0**, ZERO sentinels rendered, and the verdict is frozen at its initial placeholder - 'Computing stock health...', 'Loading day plan...', 'Computing PM compliance...' - which will never resolve. inventory additionally still shows CLEAR / STOCKED wording. THE ROOT, PRECISELY: my flags are set from `res.error` - a RESOLVED response carrying an error body. A rejected promise never produces one, so the flag stays false and the guard I added never runs; worse, the rejection propagates and aborts the init chain before the summary renders at all, which is why the verdict keeps its HTML placeholder instead of even reaching the zero branch. A 500 and a dead network arrive through two different doors and I only instrumented one. THIS IS ALSO THE STUCK-PLACEHOLDER SHAPE the same session found on skillmatrix (a persistent, correct failure toast beside a verdict reading 'Computing skill progress...' forever): nothing false is ASSERTED by a frozen 'Computing...', so an oracle hunting fabricated values passes it while a person watches a spinner that will never finish. Here it is worse, because the KPIs underneath it read 0. A toast does say 'check your connection' on these pages, so the reader is not told nothing - but the same timing evidence from this session applies: toasts on these pages fire within 150-240ms and dismiss, while the zeros persist indefinitely. TO FINISH (batched per A15, one wave, no mid-walk edits): set the same _<x>ReadFailed flag in the CATCH block each of these load functions already has (inventory.html:2214 'inventory load failed', and the equivalents on the other three), and CALL the summary renderer from that catch so the sentinel path runs even when the load threw. Then re-walk fail_offline AND fail_timeout together, since a timeout arrives through the same rejection door.

evidence.asserts: every quantity a reader could act on carries its unit; a bare number is either a count of things or prints its own denominator
evidence.checked: SETTLED BY READING EVERY FLAGGED FIGURE INDIVIDUALLY, after TWO generations of automated classifier both failed - which is why this row rests on inspection with a stated denominator rather than on a lens verdict. GEN-1 FAILED FIVE WAYS and was discarded: it flagged wizard STEP ORDINALS (1 2 3) as unit-less quantities; it lacked bare 'h' and 'year' in its vocabulary, so analytics' CORRECT 6.2h MTTR and 1-year window were called bare; it flagged BOUNDED SCORES that print their own denominator (hive readiness 62/100); and its fixed 3-level ancestor walk escaped the label region entirely, returning the PAGE TITLE as a figure's context on dayplanner. GEN-2 walks up only until a label-bearing ancestor is found and ABSTAINS when none exists (24 abstentions on dayplanner, 21 on analytics), exempts ordinals and printed-denominator scores, and widened the unit vocabulary. THEN EVERY REMAINING FLAG WAS READ BY HAND and confirmed dimensionless: '30 machines', '3 low' / '0 out', hive readiness sub-scores 100/42/70, 'Mechanical - 3 +' skill level, and per-asset failure counts (CR-001 11, GEN-001 10). THE REASON NO LENS CAN CLOSE THIS ORACLE: 'is this number dimensionless?' is a judgement about the DOMAIN, not a lexical property of the label. '30 machines' needs no unit because a machine is a thing rather than a quantity of something; '2.438' NEEDS one because vibration is measured in mm/s or in g and those differ by orders of magnitude. A keyword lens cannot make that distinction, and one that claims to is producing confident noise. THE CONTRAST WORTH RECORDING: a sweep across these pages found nothing they got wrong, while careful reading of ONE panel found the thing that matters - asset-hub renders 2.438 under a VIBRATION heading with no unit, even though v_sensor_truth carries a unit column beside value. That is filed against asset-hub, not here. ON THIS PAGE: downtime in hours, and part quantities carrying their unit of measure.

A 'number-bearing element' is defined narrowly: a LEAF element whose entire trimmed text is numeric after stripping currency, separators, % and a unit suffix - '9' and '61%' qualify, '9 open items carried over' does not because it labels itself. A label counts when it is non-numeric text of >=3 chars in the element's own aria-label/title or in an ancestor's text with the number removed, climbing at most 4 ancestors and only while that ancestor's subtree is section-sized or smaller (<=400 chars) - both bounds are load-bearing, because too tight invents defects (it once called analytics' fully-documented OEE hero unlabelled for being 35 chars too verbose) and too loose makes the pass free by accepting a whole section's prose as a label. findings.title: MEASURED with tools/prove_source_chip.mjs, live: 41 views graded across the roster - 18 make a TRUE provenance claim, 23 make NO claim, 0 name a feed they never read.
findings.detail: MEASURED with tools/prove_source_chip.mjs, live: 41 views graded across the roster - 18 make a TRUE provenance claim, 23 make NO claim, 0 name a feed they never read. THE ORACLE MATTERS MORE THAN MOST UI TEXT: a source chip is a promise that a number came from named feeds, and a reader uses it to decide whether to trust the figure. A chip naming a feed the page never queried is worse than no chip, because it manufactures confidence. SO THE CLAIM IS CHECKED AGAINST THE NETWORK, not the source: every PostgREST /rest/v1/<relation> the view actually requests is captured at runtime, and each schema-shaped token the chip names must correspond to one. It is deliberately ONE-DIRECTIONAL - a chip that SUMMARISES is fine, a chip that INVENTS is not. ★TWO MANUFACTURED FINDINGS WERE CAUGHT AND REMOVED BEFORE ANY OF THIS WAS BANKED. The first version of the token test counted the bare word `logbook`, so asset-hub and analytics were both reported as naming an unread feed - on the strength of ordinary prose: 'Based on your asset records, risk scores, logbook, failure analysis'. That is a sentence describing FEATURES to a person, not an assertion about a table, and analytics is right on its own terms - it reads analytics_snapshots, a snapshot DERIVED from logbook data, which is precisely what 'saved snapshot ... based on your logbook' says. A keyword match over human prose is how a page's own helper text becomes a defect. The test now counts a token only when it is unmistakably schema-shaped (a v_ prefix, a _truth suffix, or a known table prefix + underscore); bare English words never qualify. ★AND THE VIEW IS READ INSIDE ITSELF. V1 is graded at page scope and V2 inside the OPENED view via the shared tools/dialog_targets.mjs registry, because crediting a V2 row with a V1 reading is the one-measurement-swept-two-views error this bank has already paid for once. NOT BANKED GREEN: this view displays NO source chip at all (0 on screen while the surface requested 10 relation(s)). A surface that makes no provenance claim has not made a TRUE one, and the oracle asks whether the claim is true - so silence cannot satisfy it. Scoring it green would credit the absence of a promise as a kept promise. THIS IS ALSO NOT AUTOMATICALLY A DEFECT. Most of the 23 are V2 dialogs - a composer, a confirm sheet, a detail panel - which display a form rather than a derived figure, and a provenance chip on a surface that states no number would be noise. WHAT SETTLES IT is the per-view question the bank actually asks: does THIS view show a figure a reader would want provenance for? If yes, the chip is missing and this is a real finding; if no, the row is declared-na under R10 with 'this view states no derived figure' as the reason and the CM comprehension oracles as its replacement. Left owed rather than guessed, because that question is per-view and answering it from a count would be inventing the verdict.

findings.detail: MEASURED BY ACTUALLY DOING IT with tools/prove_effect_visible.mjs, then reading the effect back with psql as postgres - the only reader that cannot be fooled by the page's own cache. A maintenance entry was captured through the page's OWN path, addEntry(), carrying a marker string no human would type. ★THE PAGE VALIDATES ITS OWN CAPTURE CONTRACT AND THE PROBE READS THAT VERDICT: addEntry runs whValidateCapture(db,'logbook_add_entry_v1',payload) and returns {ok:false, reason:'capture_violation', errors} when a payload is wrong. So a refusal is reported AS a refusal with its reason and can never be mistaken for a failed write - the exact confusion that nearly produced a false defect on dayplanner, where I called a no-argument save function with an object and the page correctly refused an empty form. This run returned 'saved'. WRITE DISCIPLINE: the restore mechanism was teeth-tested on a real row before this prover was allowed to write (a mutation was applied, PROVEN to have landed, then reverted byte-identical). Cleanup runs in `finally` and is VERIFIED by re-count - this run left 0 rows behind. NOT BANKED EITHER WAY - THE SURFACE READING IS INCONCLUSIVE, AND SAYING SO IS THE POINT. The marker was NOT found on screen immediately, so the probe reloaded and looked again; it was not found after the reload either. That LOOKS like a clean defect - written to the database, never shown to the person who wrote it. It is not, and the number that gives it away is bodyChars: 1123. This page renders several thousand characters when it has loaded; 1,123 is a tenth of that. THE PAGE HAD NOT FINISHED RENDERING inside the probe's wait window, so the second look measured the WAIT, not the product. A one-shot text scan cannot tell 'the surface does not show this' from 'the surface has not drawn yet', and only one of those is a defect. Recording a red here would have been the stuck-skeleton class in reverse - blaming a page for a probe that looked too early. The active filter at that moment was captured too (["\ud83d\udc77Supervisor"]), because logbook opens in a role-scoped view for this identity and a fresh personal entry can legitimately sit behind a view switch - a second, independent reason a true entry may be off-screen. WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT: wait on a READINESS SIGNAL rather than a fixed timeout (the entry list having rendered any row at all), then assert the marker; and switch to 'My Entries' before looking, so the filter cannot hide a true effect. Both are small and concrete - this is a probe to sharpen, not a product to fix.

evidence.asserts: repeating an identical write does not create a second record, and the guarantee is enforced by a constraint rather than by the client
evidence.checked: PROVEN BY REPEATING THE WRITE, inside BEGIN ... ROLLBACK as an authenticated member. The same row - same primary key, same payload - was inserted twice in one transaction. The second attempt was refused: 'duplicate key value violates unique constraint logbook_pkey'. So a repeat cannot create a second record, and the guarantee comes from a CONSTRAINT rather than from client-side de-duplication that a double-tap, a retry, or an offline queue drain could outrun. WHY THE CONSTRAINT IS THE RIGHT PLACE FOR IT: this platform queues field-capture writes offline and drains them on reconnect, so the same logical write can genuinely arrive twice from two directions. A uniqueness guarantee that lives in the page dies with the page's assumptions; one that lives in the index holds for the queue drain, the retry and the second tab alike. VERIFIED CLEAN: 0 probe rows survived. ANCHORED ON supabase/migrations PER A13. SCOPE: this settles the REPEAT of an identical write. It does not settle a second write with a DIFFERENT client-generated id representing the same intent - that is the offline-queue collapse question and lives on its own seam row.
evidence.value_checked: second identical insert refused by logbook_pkey; 0 rows after rollback

findings.title: MEASURED AND FAILING - 4 of 4 user-triggered write(s) on this page fire with NO connectivity check before them: submitAsset (listener-bound), deleteAsset, saveEditAsset, saveEditFromForm (listener-bound).
findings.detail: MEASURED AND FAILING - 4 of 4 user-triggered write(s) on this page fire with NO connectivity check before them: submitAsset (listener-bound), deleteAsset, saveEditAsset, saveEditFromForm (listener-bound). THE PREMISE WAS CHECKED FIRST, because filing this against a page that is guarded elsewhere would be a manufactured finding: utils.js already defines whRequireOnline(action, notify) and exposes it as window.whRequireOnline, and it already carries the exact sentence this oracle asks for - 'You are offline. <action> needs a connection - nothing was sent, so nothing is half-done.' The scanner's GUARD pattern matches RequireOnline( and navigator.onLine === false, so a page that called either would have counted as guarded. None of these writes call anything. This is NON-ADOPTION of a centralized, correctly-worded helper, not a missing message. WHY THE PLATFORM'S EXISTING GREEN DOES NOT COVER THIS: tools/validate_offline_write_guard.py PASSES at fail-severity, but its PAGES list is exactly ['marketplace.html', 'marketplace-seller.html'] - 19 writes on two pages. None of the 22 roster pages is in its scope, so its green says nothing about them. And widening that list alone would NOT be enough: the validator's user_invokable() recognises only window.X = and inline onclick/onchange/onsubmit, so of the 53 exposed writes measured across the roster it would see 37 and miss the 16 bound with addEventListener. WHAT A PASSIVE BANNER DOES NOT DO, since every page already adopts one: the banner states the condition, it does not refuse the action. The button still fires, the request still leaves, and the person still cannot tell whether their work landed - which is the whole distinction this oracle draws. THE FIX IS ONE LINE PER WRITE at the top of each function - if (!whRequireOnline('<gerund>', showToast)) return; - and the highest-stakes ones on this page should go first. WHAT THE NEXT WALK NEEDS after the guards land: prove it LIVE rather than statically, and note that setOffline does not flip navigator.onLine in the page, so the probe must override navigator.onLine AND block the network, then assert that zero requests fired and the sentence reached the person.

findings.title: LEFT OWED BECAUSE THE ORACLE AS WORDED DOES NOT DESCRIBE THIS WRITE, and forcing it either way would be the false reading.
findings.detail: LEFT OWED BECAUSE THE ORACLE AS WORDED DOES NOT DESCRIBE THIS WRITE, and forcing it either way would be the false reading. The oracle asks that offline 'the write is refused BEFORE firing and the person is told NOTHING WAS SENT'. A logbook entry is field capture, and field capture on this platform is designed to QUEUE - so the honest offline behaviour here is the opposite of a refusal, and banking this green would credit a refusal that must not exist while banking it red would call a working feature a defect. A live attempt was made and could not reach the composer field from the default view (the reach tried #entry-text / #log-text / a generic textarea and a 'new entry' opener); the capture modal has to be opened explicitly first. That is a reach gap, not a page defect. findings.title: OWED, WITH THE REACH NOW MAPPED IN DETAIL - and with a correction to my own earlier reading on this row, because I twice came close to filing a serious false defect here.
findings.detail: OWED, WITH THE REACH NOW MAPPED IN DETAIL - and with a correction to my own earlier reading on this row, because I twice came close to filing a serious false defect here. THE ORACLE STILL DOES NOT FIT THIS WRITE. A logbook entry is field capture and this page queues it: the create path has an offline branch (queueEntryOffline(payload), the entry unshifted into _allEntries marked _offline:true, updateOfflineBadge(), the sync badge revealed, a toast), and the edit path re-queues via put() on the id keyPath so an offline create-then-edit REPLACES the pending insert rather than adding a second - this page's own collapse-to-one-row invariant, implemented. So 'refused before firing / nothing was sent' is the wrong requirement; green would credit a refusal that must not exist and red would call a working feature a defect. A sibling `offline_queued` cell is proposed in PAGE_TESTBANK_ROADMAP.md SS6, and tools/prove_offline_queued.mjs now exists to grade it. WHAT THE LIVE ATTEMPT ESTABLISHED, none of which was known before and all of which the next walk needs: (1) THE SAVE IS A FORM SUBMIT, NOT A BUTTON CLICK. #save-entry-btn is type="submit" and measures ZERO WIDTH in the default layout; calling .click() on it does NOT run the handler - measured with the form reporting checkValidity()===true and zero :invalid fields, the label never changed from 'Save Entry' to 'Saving...'. Submitting the form via requestSubmit() did not reach the queue either, so the submit listener needs tracing before this row can be graded. (2) THE ASSET FIELD CANNOT BE WRITTEN DIRECTLY. #f-machine is a hidden input, but selectAsset() also resolves _pendingAssetRefId to a uuid via resolveAssetNodeId - so setting the input alone leaves the page's own state unset. Go through #asset-picker-btn and click a real #asset-picker-list button[data-asset-id] row. (3) SEVERAL SELECTS MUST BE CHOSEN (f-maint-type, f-category, f-root-cause); their first option is a 'Select ...' placeholder, so take the first option with a real value. (4) DO NOT READ VALIDATION FROM BODY TEXT ON THIS PAGE. Strings like 'DISCIPLINE / CATEGORY required' and 'SYMPTOM / WHAT WAS WRONG? required' are the form's own LABELS - they are present whether or not anything is wrong, so a keyword scan for /required/ reports a validation failure that is not happening. THE TWO FALSE FINDINGS I ALMOST FILED, recorded so the next walker does not repeat them: first, a counter that had been running since page load showed 16 offline writes, which read as a write storm escaping the queue - re-run with the counter zeroed AT THE PRESS, all 16 were boot traffic and the press produced zero. Second, 'zero writes + a reassuring message' looked like a silent DROP of a worker's entry under a promise that work was safe - the control test settled it: the same press ONLINE also produced zero writes, so the save was simply never running. The sentence I had credited ('Offline: new entries will sync when connected') is the page's passive BANNER, not the save's confirmation. Both mistakes have the same shape: an absence of writes is not evidence of anything until you can show the action actually ran.

findings.detail: FAILS: with 3 reads answered 500, **this page offers no retry control at all** - zero visible elements whose label or handler mentions retry or try-again. It also renders **'No entries yet.'** while the reads have FAILED - so the page's only message is a false statement about the reader's own work history, and there is no control to correct it. SO A READER'S ONLY RECOURSE IS A FULL PAGE RELOAD, which on a phone in a plant means losing whatever was on screen and paying the whole load again on the connection that just failed. THE PLATFORM HAS THE PATTERN ALREADY, so this is unadopted rather than undesigned: community renders a toast reading 'Couldn't load the community feed. Check your connection and try again.' with a **Retry** button beside it, and public-feed's Retry was measured firing a real re-request and then rendering 15 posts. Six of the seven pages measured in this sweep have neither. WHAT WOULD PASS IT: a control that re-issues the failed read and is measurable as such - the probe counts requests fired after the click, so a button that merely re-renders the previous failure fails too. That distinction is not hypothetical: it is the exact defect commit 3ddef99d fixed on public-feed. MEASURED BY FAILING EVERY READ AT window.fetch AND COUNTING WHAT THE PAGE DOES NEXT. Each `/rest/v1/` and `/rpc/` request is answered with a synthetic 500 (`{"code":"500"}`, Content-Type application/json) while `/auth/v1/` is left untouched so the session survives - so the page sees a server fault, not a dead network, and supabase-js resolves it into an error object exactly as PostgREST would. Interceptions are counted and a verdict over zero failed reads is refused as vacuous. THE INJECTION HAD TO MOVE FROM THE TRANSPORT TO window.fetch, AND THAT MATTERS FOR TRUST. An earlier pass used Playwright's `route()` and intercepted **0** requests on all 8 pages while they rendered real data - a registered service worker sits between the page and the transport in a warm context, so route() never saw the calls. Every verdict from that pass would have been false, and the interception counter is the only reason it was caught rather than banked. AND THE READING IS GUARDED INSIDE THE EVALUATE: it refuses unless the auth token holds the expected uid, `location.pathname` still ends in this page's own file, and the body is NOT in the 13,000-16,000 char landing-page band. A previous unguarded pass returned byte-identical output for seven different pages - 14,677 chars of marketing copy - because the session had expired and every page had redirected to `index.html?signin=1`. Seven page-specific verdicts, all of them the landing page. The guard is not ceremony.

findings.title: The DB's legible rate-limit message is likely MASKED by a generic client string on the write path
findings.detail: The refusal this row banks on is excellent AT ITS SOURCE: 'You have logged today's free limit (100). Resets at midnight.' with HINT logbook_daily_user. But the client does not necessarily show it. logbook.html:1885 renders save failures as a fixed string - 'Could not save. Check your connection and try again.' - which is not only generic but WRONG for this case: the connection is fine, the person hit a daily cap, and 'try again' is the one instruction guaranteed to fail until midnight. So the platform can produce a genuinely good limit message and still tell the reader to retry immediately. This is the mirror image of a defect fixed earlier in this same session, where pages echoed the RAW upstream message to the reader: the lesson is not 'always show the server string' nor 'never show it', but that a write path needs to distinguish a LIMIT (legible, actionable, has a reset time) from a FAULT (retry may work) - and the HINT key exists precisely so it can. NOT ESCALATED TO A FAILURE on this row because the oracle asks whether the rate limit is legible, and at the layer that produces it, it is - verifiably, with a machine-readable key. TO FINISH: on the write error path, branch on the hint/SQLSTATE (logbook_daily_user, 54000) and surface the server's own sentence plus its reset time instead of the connection string. Then re-walk this oracle at the client layer.

evidence.asserts: when a limit is hit the refusal is legible - it names the limit, the scope, and when it clears, and carries a machine-readable key so a client can tell WHICH limit fired
evidence.checked: FIRED FOR REAL, NOT READ FROM THE SOURCE - and then the source was read to confirm the second tier. Inside BEGIN ... ROLLBACK as an authenticated member (role SET, not just claims), a burst of 400 logbook inserts was attempted. The trigger refused with: **'You have logged today's free limit (100). Resets at midnight.'** carrying HINT 'logbook_daily_user'. Verified clean afterwards: 0 probe rows survived the rollback. WHY THIS COUNTS AS LEGIBLE, CLAUSE BY CLAUSE: it names the LIMIT (100), names WHAT was hit (today's free limit, i.e. a per-user daily cap rather than a system fault), tells the reader WHEN IT CLEARS ('Resets at midnight') so they know whether to wait or escalate, and ships a machine-readable HINT key ('logbook_daily_user') so a client can branch on WHICH limit fired instead of pattern-matching English. That combination - human sentence plus stable key - is what separates a legible limit from 'permission denied'. THERE IS A SECOND TIER AND IT IS ALSO LEGIBLE: check_hive_quota_logbook raises 'logbook cumulative quota exceeded for hive % (% >= %)' with ERRCODE 54000 and a HINT that old records can be archived - so the per-user daily cap and the per-hive cumulative quota are distinguishable by SQLSTATE and by message, and the hive-level one tells the reader the remedy (archive) rather than just the fact. ANCHORED ON supabase/migrations PER A13 - the message lives in the trigger body.
